model.name: Stray Component & Variable Finder (Ghost, Unindexed, Orphaned, Etc.)
model.description:
What is this plugin good for?


This plugin makes it easy to identify ‘stray’ component or variables within a design file.


What is a ‘stray' component/variable

A stray component or variable is one that either:

(1) is no longer properly linked to its original library (because the library was removed or changed), or

(2) was left behind from a previous library you no longer want to use.


Figma often identifies these in your assets panel as libraries that are ‘used in this file’ but they does not give you any indication of WHERE in the file they are being used. This plugin makes it easy to identify these components.


𖨠𖨠𖨠 If you find this plugin useful, and you feel like it, throw me some coffee dollars. 𖨠𖨠𖨠


How do I use this plugin?


1. Identify libraries you want to keep.

Start by opening the file where you want to find and fix stray components or variables. In the Assets panel, review the libraries that are currently being used in the file.


2. Index the libraries you don't want flagged as stray.

Open the plugin inside each library file you want to keep.

In the Library Manager tab, click "Index Library" for each one.

This ensures that components and variables from these libraries won't be flagged as stray later.


3. Return to your target file and run a scan.

Go back to your target file. In the plugin, open the "Scan Components/Variables" tab and choose whether you want to scan for components or variables.

The plugin will search your file for anything not included in your indexed libraries.


4. Review the results.

You'll see a list of all stray components or variables it found, along with helpful details like node names and their location in the file.





More Specific FAQ Questions 


What is the difference between Variable View and Node View for variables?


Variable View:

Organizes the scan results by each specific stray variable.

You can see all the places across your file where a particular stray variable appears.


Node View:

Organizes the scan results by the nodes that have the most stray variables.

This helps you prioritize fixing nodes with the highest number of issues, regardless of the variable types.


The scan is identifying components that belong to one of my indexed libraries as a Stray, what’s going on?


The most likely answer is that the component was deleted from the library. When this happens the component in the target file will point to its original library but does not actually exist there any longer (and therefore was not indexed)


Why can’t the plugin identify the library the stray component/variable comes from?


The Figma Plugin API does not expose data about files you own or have access to, so there is no way to get this information without adding an Authentication flow


Why can’t the plugin display the name of each variable in the results list?


Similar to the answer above, the Plugin API cannot get the name of variables from files that it does not have access to. It can only access the local name of the variable which tends to be semantically meaningless. Sorry.


Can I scan for both components and variables at the same time?


No, you’ll need to run the scan separately for components and variables. Maybe this could come in a future update.


Do I need to re-index libraries if they change?


Yes. If you update a library (e.g. delete or rename components/variables), it's a good idea to re-open that file and click “Index Library” again to make sure your scan stays accurate.


How long does the scan take?


The indexing and scanning process should be relatively quick (~3 to 30 seconds) generally; however the processing time is related to how big of a file you are scanning.

model.name: Variable Chain Visualiser
model.description:
Variable Chain Visualiser

See how your variables really connect.


What it does


Figma variables often point to other variables instead of holding a value on their own. A button color might point to a brand color, which points to a base color, which finally points to a hex code. This is called aliasing, and it is how most design systems are built today.


The problem is that these chains are invisible in Figma's own panel. As a file grows past a few dozen variables, nobody can see the full picture anymore. Broken links, unused variables, and confusing chains build up quietly, and nobody notices until something breaks on screen.


Alias Chain Visualizer scans your whole file in one pass and lays out every chain so you can actually see it.


Features


See the full picture

Every variable in your file, shown in one view. Primitive values, semantic tokens, and component variables, laid out side by side so you can trace how they connect.


Trace any chain

Click on any variable to follow its full path, from the raw value all the way up to where it is used.


Find what is broken

The plugin checks for five common problems in your file:


Broken links, where a variable points to something that no longer exists

Loops, where a chain circles back on itself

Unused variables, that nothing else in the file references

Chains that go too deep, making them hard to follow or maintain

Values that stop working in certain modes


Check every mode

Switch between Light, Dark, or any other mode your file uses, and see if a variable still resolves the way it should in each one.


See what depends on it

Click into any variable to see every component that uses it. Know exactly what you would affect before you make a change.


Read-only, always

The plugin only looks at your file. It never edits, renames, or deletes anything. You stay fully in control of every change.


Why it helps


Design systems get harder to trust as they grow. A small typo or a missed link can sit inside a chain for months before anyone notices it in the actual design. This plugin gives you a way to check your file on your own terms, instead of finding problems by accident later.


It also makes onboarding easier. New team members can open the plugin and see how the whole token system fits together, instead of clicking through dozens of variables one at a time.


Who it is for


Designers who maintain a variable library and want to understand what they are changing before they change it

Design system leads who run periodic checks to keep the file healthy

Teams handing off a design system to someone new, who need a fast way to explain how it works


How it works


Open the plugin, run a scan, and browse the results. There is no setup, no configuration, and nothing to connect. It works entirely inside the file you already have open.

model.name: Variable Audit
model.description:
Design systems make it easy to answer "where is this variable used?" The harder question is the opposite one: where should a variable have been used, and wasn't? That is the hardcoded #0D99FF on a button, the magic 24px gap, the raw corner radius someone typed in a hurry.


Variable Audit scans your file and answers three questions.



COVERAGE: what is missing

A single adoption score, broken down by category (color, spacing, radius, stroke, typography), by page, and by top-level frame, so you can say "Checkout is at 34%" instead of guessing.


The score separates variables from styles, because a file can score well on color and text styles while using no variables at all. If nothing is bound to a variable, the plugin says so plainly rather than letting styles flatter the number.


Every hardcoded value is listed and ranked by how often it appears, each matched to the variable it should have been. Matches respect variable scopes, so a corner radius token is never suggested for a fill, and every suggestion carries a confidence level. Click any finding to jump straight to the layer.



USAGE: where your variables actually are

A complete map of every binding: which variable, which property, which page, frame and layer. Search it, expand any variable to see its layers, click a row to select that layer on canvas, or select every layer using a variable at once. Run this before renaming or changing a token, so you know what you are about to affect.



CLEANUP: what is actually safe to remove

Local variables that nothing in the file reaches.


Unlike a naive scan, this follows alias chains, so a primitive referenced only by a semantic token is never reported as deletable. Hidden layers are always searched for usage, which means hiding a layer never makes its token look unused.



SCAN WHAT YOU NEED

Scope a run to the whole file, the current page, or just your selection.

Selection and page scans return in seconds, so you can check a frame while you work. A 500,000 layer design system takes a few minutes for a full pass, stays responsive throughout, and any scan can be cancelled part way.



EXPORTS

Everything downloads as CSV: coverage by page and frame, untokenized values with their suggested tokens, per layer detail, the full usage map, and cleanup candidates.



DETAILS

Light, dark and automatic themes, with your choice remembered between runs.


No network access at all. The manifest forbids it, so nothing leaves your machine and nothing is collected. The plugin never writes to your file: suggestions are reported, not applied.



ONE HONEST LIMITATION

Figma gives plugins no way to see whether other files use a variable, so anything published to a library is flagged in the cleanup list. Treat that list as "investigate these", not "delete these".

model.description:
Description

Figma Quality Guardian is a comprehensive pre-ship audit for your Figma files — it scans your design against 7 categories of real-world quality checks, explains exactly why each issue matters, and fixes what's safely fixable, all without your file ever leaving Figma.

Design QA today is manual, inconsistent, and easy to skip under deadline pressure. Quality Guardian turns it into a repeatable, one-click check: run an audit, get a Release Readiness Score, work through a prioritized issue list, and ship knowing nothing slipped through.

Every issue is explained in plain language — what it is, why it matters, and what to do about it. Where a fix is deterministic and safe, Quality Guardian applies it for you, one at a time or in bulk, with a full before/after preview. Everything runs through Figma's native undo, so nothing is ever a one-way door.

Analysis runs 100% inside Figma, using only the Plugin API — no account, no network calls, no AI, no data collection. One license, every feature unlocked.

Built for designers who want a second pair of eyes before every ship, and for teams who want design QA to be a checklist item, not a hope.

Features

Scanning

•3 scan scopes — Current Selection, Current Page, or Entire File

•Chunked, cancellable scanning with a live progress bar, so large files don't freeze the UI

•7 audit categories, each independently toggleable before a scan

Design System (10 rules)

•Hard-coded colors that match an existing Variable (offers to bind it) or Paint Style (offers to apply it), or match nothing registered at all

•Off-scale Auto Layout spacing/padding, font size, and corner radius (each with a "round to nearest scale value" fix)

•Near-duplicate Paint Styles (within 12 RGB units)

•Unused local Variables

•Generic/auto-generated component names

•3+ standalone components that share a naming pattern and likely belong in one component set

•Possible detached component instances (heuristic)

Content (13 rules)

•Spelling (curated ~100-entry misspelling list) with one-click fix

•US/UK English consistency, checked against your project's configured variant (~85 word pairs)

•Terminology consistency across true UI synonyms (Log in/Sign in, OK/Okay, etc.), correctable toward your preferred term

•Grammar: subject/verb agreement, passive voice detection

•UX writing: redundant/wordy phrasing, unnecessary "please," weak CTA wording ("Click here," generic "Submit")

•Repeated words, double spaces, missing terminal punctuation, overly long sentences

•Placeholder/TODO markers, Lorem Ipsum, empty text layers

•Inconsistent capitalization style across short labels/buttons

Accessibility (6 rules)

•WCAG 2.1 contrast ratio checking (AA or AAA, your choice), against the nearest solid-fill ancestor background

•Text below a configurable minimum size

•Touch targets below a configurable minimum size on interactive elements

•Icon-only interactive elements with no text label

•Heading-level skips (H1 → H3, etc.)

•Flags when contrast can't be automatically determined, so nothing is silently skipped

Localization (5 rules)

•Expansion-risk simulation per target language (German, French, Spanish, Italian, Finnish, Japanese, Chinese, Arabic) using published expansion ratios

•Overflow risk for fixed-width text, buttons, and nav/menu items specifically

•RTL review flag when Arabic is a target language

Responsive / Layout (8 rules)

•Fixed-size text that won't grow with its content

•Children overflowing non-Auto-Layout parent bounds

•Inconsistent Auto Layout usage or spacing across same-named sibling frames

•Absolute positioning inside an Auto Layout parent

•Default/never-customized constraints on frames above a size threshold

•Weak signal for missing mobile layouts (no small frame anywhere in scope)

File Health (7 rules)

•Empty frames/groups, hidden layers, redundant single-child group wrappers

•Unused components and styles (zero references in scope)

•Excessive nesting depth

•Duplicate-named sibling layers

•Guided cleanup flow: select flagged layers and delete them in bulk, gated behind an explicit confirmation dialog naming exactly what's removed

Handoff (4 rules)

•Generic layer names on non-component layers

•Text with no linked text style

•Component sets with only one variant (possibly missing states)

•Same-named siblings with inconsistent opacity

Fixing

•Safe, one-click auto-fix for every deterministic rule (word replacement, style/variable binding, spacing/font-size rounding, layer renaming)

•Bulk "Fix All" across everything currently filtered

•Before/after preview on every fixable issue

•Every fix is a normal document edit — undo with Cmd/Ctrl+Z, no custom undo stack

Reporting & Scoring

•Release Readiness Score (0–100) with category breakdown and a rating band (Excellent/Good/Needs Improvement/Not Ready)

•Filterable, paginated Issue Explorer (severity, category, status, auto-fixable-only)

•Branded PDF export with a gradient logo banner, color-coded score badge, and full issue tables

•CSV export of the full report

•Per-issue "Select in Figma" to jump straight to the layer

Settings & Configuration

•Configurable thresholds (min font size, touch target size, long-sentence word count, nesting depth)

•English variant (US/UK), accessibility standard (AA/AAA), terminology preferences

•Persisted locally via figma.clientStorage; ignored-issue list persists across scans

model.description:
Green Lens scans your Figma selection and scores it against real sustainability patterns from the Green Software Foundation — covering typography, media, color, device longevity, and data handling — then gives you one-click actions to actually fix what it finds, not just a list of complaints.


What it checks


  1. Typography — flags custom fonts that could be system fonts, excessive font weights/styles, too many font families, and body text set in a custom font where a system font would do. Scoped to text inside actual screen-sized frames, so designer notes and annotations don't skew results.
  2. Media & Assets — catches images that are far larger than their display size (with a one-click "Resize & re-import" that actually downscales and swaps the fill, or a lighter "Set export to Nx" for just the export setting), suggests WebP downloads generated right in the plugin, flags duplicate images that aren't yet componentized, and calls out autoplay/looping video.
  3. Color & Palette — flags gradients on large fills, one-off colors with no linked style (with a button that either links to your closest existing style or creates and links a new one automatically), unused/orphaned styles, visually near-duplicate colors worth merging, near-white backgrounds on your main screen frame, and whether a dark-mode variant exists.
  4. Device Longevity — checklist-style signals on responsive layout usage, low-end viewport coverage, heavy blur/shadow density, and animation complexity — flagged as things worth verifying, not scored, since a static file can't confirm real device behavior.
  5. Data Handling — checklist prompts around form field count, tracking/consent UI, caching-friendly asset reuse, and unpaginated long lists.


How it works


Scan is scoped to whatever frame, section, component, or instance you've selected — not the whole file — and skips hidden layers entirely.

A live progress bar shows exactly which category is being scanned.

Every finding can be selected on canvas with one click; many come with a further action — resize an image, download it as WebP, or link a stray color straight to a style/variable — and mark themselves done once applied.

Scores are transparently labeled as estimated heuristics, not measured carbon output, with a five-round grounding in GSF's actual sustainability principles (Carbon Efficiency, Energy Efficiency, Hardware Efficiency, Carbon Awareness, Measurement).

model.name: Coverset — Component Audit: Used Variants, Unused Combinations, Instances & Bulk Swap
model.description:
Coverset reads every instance of your components and tells you which versions are actually in use, which of the possible combinations have never been used once, and where each one lives. Then it writes the answer back into your file.


YOUR IT REVIEW CAN CHECK THIS, NOT TAKE MY WORD

Coverset declares no network access, and Figma prints that on this page beside the last-updated date — so the person who approves plugins where you work can confirm it without contacting me. Your components are already in your file: there is nothing to upload and nothing to sign in to. Nothing about your work leaves your machine — including how you use the plugin, which is not measured either. There is nothing to fill in on a security questionnaire, and no service that can go down and take the plugin with it.


WHAT YOUR FILE ACTUALLY USES

A component with a few properties has an enormous number of possible combinations, and a file normally uses a small part of that space. Coverset counts both sides — the combinations in use and the combinations never used — and shows the coverage for each component set, and for the file as a whole. It is a figure about your file, not a verdict on it: a version nobody has used yet is not called a mistake anywhere in this plugin.


ALL FIVE KINDS OF PROPERTY

Figma has five kinds of component property: variant, boolean, text, instance swap and slot. Only two of them can be listed from the component definition alone, so counting that way can never reach the other three. Coverset counts what is used instead, which is why text and swapped instances are in the totals as well. That is not typed in by hand — a test reads Figma's own type definitions and fails if the two ever disagree.


DECISIONS, NOT ROWS

"Size=M, Type=Rich, Bold=on, used here" is one row with the count on it, however many instances it stands for. Values shared by every row move up into the heading, so the part that actually differs is what you read. A whole file becomes a list you can go through before you agree to anything.


NARROW IT DOWN

Type part of a name or a property value and the list narrows to the versions that carry it — the set name is often the same on every row, so the values are what you are actually looking for. Alongside it are the things only the counts can tell you: versions nested inside other components, hidden ones, ones Figma reports overrides on, ones from a library, local ones, ones whose main component is gone, and ones used exactly once. What you have narrowed to is also what the buttons act on, and anything ticked that falls outside the filter is named and left alone rather than quietly changed.


THE WHOLE FILE, AND A STOP BUTTON

Scan the selection, the current page, or every page. Progress and what is left are shown while it runs, and you can stop it — whatever was already read stays on screen.


WHEN IT CANNOT READ SOMETHING, IT SAYS SO

Some component sets carry errors that Figma itself refuses to describe. Coverset puts those sets at the top of the list, by name, in Figma's own words, instead of quietly counting them as zero. Every write is read back afterwards, and anything that did not take is named with the reason.


TABLES OF WHAT IS USED, OR OF WHAT IS NOT

Turn any component set into a labelled table: the versions in use, or the combinations that have never been used, laid out with their property values. You choose which, and the count is shown before anything is placed — never the whole combination space by surprise. A table is made of real instances, so building one moves your own coverage figures. Coverset tells you that rather than hiding it.


BULK SWAP

Pick the versions you want moved and send every instance of them to another version in one go. Rows go through whole or not at all — half a swapped row would leave your file worse than untouched.


FREE AND PAID

Looking is free, for ever: scan any page or the whole file, see the coverage, the used versions, the unused combinations, the overrides Figma reports, and where every instance sits. Writing is the part that costs. The first 50 writes are free across every file you open, and a row is always done whole or not at all — so a row larger than the writes you have left is named, and left untouched, rather than half done. $5 once unlocks unlimited writing, together with tables of several sets at once, exposed nested properties inside the table, and table styling bound to your local variables. One payment, no subscription.
